name: Hydrochlorothiazide

lead: Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) is a widely prescribed water pill that some forum users discuss as a milder, daily alternative to stronger loop diuretics for a less puffy, more defined face.

It blocks the sodium-chloride cotransporter in the kidney, so less sodium and water are reabsorbed and more leave in the urine. Effects start within about 2 hours and last roughly 6-12 hours. It has been sold since 1959 and is used for high blood pressure and fluid retention; no clinical study has tested it for facial puffiness.

paras: It is a prescription tablet, usually taken once daily in its medical use. In forum discussion it is framed as a gentler everyday option compared with furosemide, with the water-loss effect starting the same day.

Documented effects include low potassium, sodium and magnesium, high uric acid and calcium, raised blood sugar and lipids, and sun sensitivity. Regulators in Australia and the US highlighted a link to non-melanoma skin cancer in 2020. It is prescription-only and prohibited by WADA.

forums.title: hydrochlorothiazide is apparently a much safer and better alternative of furosemide

angle.text: Some forum users take hydrochlorothiazide as a daily water pill aimed at a less puffy, more defined face. It makes the kidneys excrete more sodium and water, so less fluid is retained. It is a common blood-pressure drug and has not been studied for appearance.

lead: Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) is a thiazide diuretic used to treat high blood pressure, edema from heart failure and other conditions, and sometimes to reduce kidney stone recurrence. It became commercially available in 1959, is on the WHO Essential Medicines List, and was the 18th most prescribed drug in the US in 2024, according to Wikipedia.[1]

It acts on the distal convoluted tubule to increase excretion of sodium and water. Commonly reported adverse effects are electrolyte disturbances, raised uric acid and blood glucose, and photosensitivity; regulators highlighted a risk of non-melanoma skin cancer in 2020.[1]
In looksmaxxing forums, users have asked whether HCTZ is a safer daily alternative to furosemide for water retention.[2] No published study has examined it for cosmetic purposes.

paras: HCTZ is used for hypertension, edema, congestive heart failure, diabetes insipidus, renal tubular acidosis and prevention of calcium kidney stones. Off-label uses include osteopenia and Meniere disease.[1] It is frequently combined with other agents such as ACE inhibitors, as in lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide tablets.[3]

The ACCOMPLISH trial compared benazepril with amlodipine against benazepril with hydrochlorothiazide in high-risk hypertensive patients.[4] An earlier MRC trial in older adults examined thiazide-based treatment of hypertension.[5] Wikipedia reports that comparisons with chlorthalidone show no clear overall difference in cardiovascular event prevention.[1]

Reported effects include low potassium, magnesium and sodium; high calcium, uric acid (with gout risk), blood sugar and lipids; headache, nausea, photosensitivity and pancreatitis.[1] Australian and US regulators highlighted non-melanoma skin cancer risk in 2020, and Wikipedia states the IARC classified it as a Group 1 carcinogen in 2024.[1]

HCTZ blocks the sodium-chloride cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule. Bioavailability is about 70%, it is minimally metabolised and mostly excreted unchanged in urine, with a half-life of roughly 6-15 hours.[1]
The World Anti-Doping Agency prohibits HCTZ because diuretics can mask other drugs; Wikipedia notes a marathon runner received a three-year ban in 2025 for its presence and use.[1]

A looksmax.org thread asked whether HCTZ is a safer, better alternative to furosemide for water retention, and a reply asked why daily use would be preferable.[2] Experience reports in the thread are sparse.

No studies found on hydrochlorothiazide for facial depuffing or other appearance goals. Clinical trials in hypertension include ACCOMPLISH and a registered single-patient comparison with lisinopril.[4][6]
